title: Federal Register: Improve Tracking of Workplace Injuries and Illnesses, final rule (OSHA)

history.reason: Source read directly on the access date; findings transcribed from the document.
Review reread clarified SBA-small entity coverage and existing versus incremental reporting scope.

publisher: U.S. Department of Labor, Occupational Safety and Health Administration (via GovInfo / Federal Register)
source_type: Government final rule with economic analysis
reliability: Government document; the issuing agency is also the party imposing or administering the requirement.
findings: Establishments with 100 or more employees in designated industries must electronically submit information from OSHA Forms 300 and 301 to OSHA once a year, in addition to the existing Form 300A submission.
OSHA states the information is already required to be kept under the existing recordkeeping regulation.

OSHA estimates the rule has economic costs of $7.7 million per year, including $7.1 million per year to the private sector, with average costs of $136 per year for affected establishments with 100 or more employees (annualized over 10 years at a 7 percent discount rate).
OSHA states the final rule is not a significant regulatory action under Executive Order 12866.

The small-entity discussion (Federal Register p. 47343) states affected establishments include SBA-defined small entities; the 100-employee establishment threshold does not exclude small businesses. Existing Form 300A submissions for certain 20+ employee establishments remain distinct.
limitations: Later OSHA actions (a 2026 rule on electronic posting appeared in a search but was not read) may change requirements.
Agency ex ante estimates; no independent measurement of actual time spent.
The $136 modeled average concerns the rule’s incremental added submission burden, not all existing OSHA recordkeeping or reporting work.
